      "id": "UgwYsSZzmKDwq0nwr1x4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "putting down my thoughts as I go through pod (basically speaking through wispr flow)\n\n- 33:35 dario is underestimating his own team, not all engineers are as good as Of Anthropic, so this, like, 100% of code written by AI is good if an engineer knows what to tell AI to write, and knowing this needs a lot of experience. Yeah, I'm repeating what most people have said many times, but still, if someone doesn't know and doesn't have that experience, their increase in productivity would be a lot less compared to one that Anthropic has with his engineers with unlimited tokens. \nAlso, there would be a bottleneck, in my opinion. Imagine anyone can prompt AI to make me a Slack and think whether the Slack made by this prompt, by an engineer who has never worked on Slack or software solutions, compared to a person who has been working on Slack for many years, knows the architecture trade-offs, etc., which would be better to use by users and sustainable. Basically, people are making these billion-dollar B2B SaaS in minutes using Claude Code, etc., but that was never the bottleneck. There have been __ from-scratch tutorials since ages, since software development has been here. No one uses those built-from-scratch products because there is a better product available and no one maintains that that simple build to match that performance, and this requires skill.\n\nAt the end, even if people are empowered too much, quite, quite much, with AI, people having these contexts of years and improving, working on it for years wouls always be ahead, yes someone new can also do that, Then he would have to keep working on the Slack that he made for a year or two so as to know what are the problems, etc., and that can't be fastened very easily, in my opinion. So basically doing end to end is very, very tough. \n\nI think we have reached the stage where it's just a skill issue for people to use these agents at their full extent. I don't think Anthropic engineers would become more productive with better models. Better tooling, etc., can help them for sure, but better models, I don't think, would improve anything in their dev routine. It would just be the tooling around that which automates a few things, etc., that would be an improvement from now onwards.\n\n\n- 37:50 no 15-20% would not expand and give avantage and believe me its not that much as well, codex is good even better at coding, also gemini would do something (please do something google)\n\n- 41:55  I am a little unsure that pre-training RL and this in-context learning would lead to Country of geniuses in a data center.\nI have this sort of hot take that it's not the context that is the problem; it's the search function in the context that is the problem. There is a very easy human analogy. A million words. Yeah, they are quite large context. The problem is, what to put, and does the model remember everything? Maybe it does. I agree on that. It takes that as a human, on-the-go learning, and has everything in that 1 million context in the model's context.\nStill, when you're working, even as an SDE, there are 5 code bases involved. There would be a time when a senior engineer would have told you, \"We have to do this this way because there is something on that code base that works like this, and if we do it this way, that would benefit us, or if we do not, this would cost us something.\" This happens all the time, but this is not the one million moving window. When I am working in SDE, working on some new feature, it's not like that one million context before this point of time contains all these things that would help me in designing the architecture. If the last 1M words before that time would contain everything needed than it would work . The human brain just instantly searches the needed information at that point of time. This is the basic magic that human brain has. What Claude Code, etc., does is it grabs, search, etc tool calls. The human brain doesn't search; it directly reaches that point when someone told something related to what I am doing right now. This is not a one million moving context window where, from this point of time, the last 1 million tokens consist of all of that critical information. That would not happen always, so would this lead to ADI? Maybe it does. I'm not sure about that. \nBasically newton can think of gravity by a falling apple, but model would just tell him not to eat it as its dirty.\n\n- 1:05:19 unless you are SSI, haha.\n\n- 2:01:13 should have asked that, still most chinese ai model are opensourced and american aren't, who is emopowering personal limitless ai agent more?\n\nsome time i just feel like I should be the third person here to discuss these things 🥲",

    {
      "id": "UgzyTSfTwb_d6UzWvBR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Don't get me wrong, I assume Dario Amodei is a very smart person, smarter than me. But I did some googling and I can't find anything that suggests he himself has any SWE experience so I'm not sure he has much experience to make such bold claims that he does. He is also a CEO and CEO's have a duty to public relations and hyping their company and product 24/7 for their shareholders, so you simply cannot believe them outright.\n\nAnthropic has paraded that they have written a C compiler entirely with AI which sounds super impressive until you engage your brain for a second and realize, a c compiler (if not multiple was certainly part of it's training data, and the resulting c compiler it made was inarguably worse than compilers already out there and that it took an intense amount of structure and defined testing and hand holding to make it happen. \"Woo, look at this, your jobs are over because we were able to make it do a thing that has already existed for 50 years\"\n\nCursor also recently supposedly made a whole browser with only a team of agents, except, it was barely a browser, couldn't even run browser tests to see how much of the standard it covers and was FULL of literally stolen code, right from Ladybird.\n\nThis reveals the problem which is obvious to anyone who has a middling understanding of how LLMs work. They don't create, they can only infer based on training data weights and context. There are not many browsers and basically one in Rust so when it had to build one in Rust, it had no choice but to steal code because it cannot, *actually*, create.\n\nWhat  LLM's are FANTASTIC for is, SWE's steal code all the time already. LLM's are just better at it. Even when making something brand new, a huge chunk of the code is going to be incredibly similar to something that has existed before. That's why stackoverflow was so successful for so long, it was a place to grab useful proven snippets of functionality that SWE's could plug together like lego to build things. In many automation tasks, there might be absolutely nothing unique about the task and an LLM can easily do it flawlessly. However, if you are actually innovating or doing something new, you will find out how actually completely unusable LLM's become in that space. What I'm finding out is that so many SWEs do not work with innovate new code... which is why I think so many people get duped into thinking LLM's are capable of more than they are",

      "parent": "Ugx1w_yYSGB1_4GXrh54AaABAg.ATBc_VFiF4xATCZDcrDydh",
      "text": "Define for us what is AGI then. Personally, I see the current multimodal models as the first AGI systems. Are these models general? Yes. But are they highly competent in those tasks? Not yet. These AGI models aren’t ASI. I think the conversation should move to ASI now, which will just be the much smarter AGI systems that have yet to be built.",

      "author_id": "UCJC2BrHPNyqmbWw01qBfXdg",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mtT7WnjlmhNn2krmYcVBC9xHJlgbbDr-yRjBAnbyizFg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugx1w_yYSGB1_4GXrh54AaABAg.ATBc_VFiF4xATCsoyq0A9D",
      "parent": "Ugx1w_yYSGB1_4GXrh54AaABAg.ATBc_VFiF4xATClTJ2_wD1",
      "text": "​ @featherfiend9095  First of all I think the term AGI is rubbish. It is supposed to mean mimicking human intelligence but there is nothing \"general\" about human intelligence. Due to evolution, human thinking is highly specialized. Calling it aGi exhibits the kind of human-centric hubris in the western culture.\n\nSecond, all the SOTA models are domain specialized. The models that are good at Go can't play chess; the models that are good at manipulating languages can't play Go. They don't generalize out of distribution. So there goes the \"G\". \nThey do something that appears to be reasoning but in fact is not reasoning at all as a couple of published papers have shown in recent months(which is totally unsurprising if one knows the inner work of those models). \n\nMost importantly, humans don't function by \"reasoning\" most of the time. AND reasoning is not just a set of logical steps to reach an answer. If it were, philosophers who use logic would all come to the same conclusion.\n The right hemisphere is far more important than the left hemisphere. It's how people understand maths, physics and all the other complex subjects on the intuitive level yet the tech bros have put zero effort into understanding & modeling how the right hemisphere works with the left hemisphere to achieve genuine understanding. They just throw data and compute at statistical models and pray magic to happen.\nI could go on but the missing pieces for AGI is far too many for this tiny space to contain.",

      "author_id": "UCNZX-3aomIHIZMfk8Ynq59g",

      "text": "​ @richardmorton2480 what an ignorant comment. AI was originally developed as a way to mathematically model the biophysics of the brain. Basic concept in biophysics is macro-scale behavior emerges from micro-scale interactions. PhD level biophysics involves high level computational modeling which is exactly what AI is. Dario literally wrote his thesis on network-scale electrophysiology and the collective behavior of neural circuits.     {
      "id": "UgzUtkUyr4bejh2ukWd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "One of the reasons some orgs are not seeing macro gains has to do with several things, learning curve, adapting existing systems which often needs custom tooling, skill variance across teams due to lack of standardized workflows with new tools and the biggest one is simply time scale, it takes much longer than most people expect to adapt to a completely new paradigm and you will stumble along the way. The studies that are out are tiny in sample size with very short time scales so there is no 'lessons learned' yet with using the tools and using dated far less capable models in these studies people cite. Still massive room for improvement for every aspect of these models but not even remotely as bad in enterprise settings as some doomers are pushing.",

      "id": "Ugz7-072pGId7y17rOJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The real financial issue is whether competitors will come along with much lower costs - cheaper, higher performance GPUs and maybe new algorithms and then under cut the pricing models for this generation of AI.  So if chips come out that are twice as powerful at half the price and models get trained at 1/4 the cost, then that company can sell the same services for 1/4 the price and therefore Anthropic (built on overly expensive Nvidia chips) would never be able to get an ROI or even payback the investment.  With such rapid advances in compute happening so fast, it is very difficult to predict where this will end up.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCeFK4yZ5z2ld92gZ2pYAHpQ",
      "author": "@lawrencesmith9059",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lHoc4SBlbAzaxSUCtByVmIScm5dnq41avP96zynS4=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyxjYXC2MtYod3zGkB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I am coming from this from a historiographical perspective more than anything, but it seems like Dario is attempting to launder the Fukayamaist position that representative democracy and capitalism are forever interlocked as the best combination of political and economic organisation, while at the same time saying that capitalism will end and this new economic system will replace it but it'll retain liberalist principles just because... he likes them i guess? The last time this happened, when capitalism was first attempted in the Netherlands and England in the mid 1600s, it was followed not by an age of widespread social upheaval and liberation, but by the literal Age of Absolutism, where monarchs across europe quite literally consolidated absolute power, where colossal nation-states were directed under the power of one person, ending in the most powerful form of authoritarianism ever attempted in the history of humanity. It was the overthrow of this horrifically repressive political system during the age of revolutions that lead to capitalism becoming the dominant form of economic organisation, not the other way around. Unless you can give some sort of evidence that this time it's going to be magically different (despite the overwhelming rise of anti-democratic hypernationalism in every single representative democracy on the face of the earth right now implying the exact opposite), I think that the rise of AI is simply going to allow the hyper-rich countries that invent it to become just that: even more fantastically wealthy, and nothing more. China right now is living proof that you don't need civil liberties to have a healthy, fast growing, extremely productive economy just as capable of making the line go up as anywhere else. In my opinion, societies that are unable to manage the large wealth inequalities that disruptive technologies and hyper-productive economic systems naturally create are the ones that do not survive, because that's exactly what happened last time, and the time before that, and the time before that.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCo8MjGD0xiGXH7Y1_YJdaDw",

      "id": "UgxTOPg2XvjOQSAfBZV4AaABAg.ATBLlRRdyEQATBM9JmbIo6",
      "parent": "UgxTOPg2XvjOQSAfBZV4AaABAg",
      "text": "You can stack another multiplier on top of this.\nEven English text input is still slow — I find voice is ~3× faster.\n\nSo if intent→code is ~100×,\nadding voice gets you closer to ~300×,\nand a future BCI could plausibly push that toward ~1000×.\n\nEach layer removes more interface friction between thought and execution.",

      "id": "UgzDhFcwu1nPNSLPnZ14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "AI CEO saying AI is great, shocking. There are these cherry-picked \"benchmarks\". So I'll cherry-pick my own:\n- LLMs still cannot accurately tell you how many R's are in \"strawberry\", which the average 7 year old can do\n- LLMs will forget what you just told it to do, which the average 7 year old won't do\n- LLMs still have to \"search the internet\" for most answers, which the average 7 year old is capable of\n- LLMs fundamentally cannot \"learn\", which any human is capable of\n- LLMs require enormous amounts of human-generated data to be kind of useful, they aren't coming up with this \"knowledge\" out of thin air\n- LLMs are fundamentally built for non-deterministic answers and built to confidently hallucinate, which means there is zero trust in the answers\n- LLMs have to consume ungodly amounts of resources for these lackluster results\n\nI still don't see the hype. Even if you were to believe these psychopaths, their \"utopia\" is that humans are replaced.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Ahhh... Code is not \"PhD+\" level, whatever that means. Unless someone is far beyond Opus 4.6 and I'm not aware of it, Claude is very much a junior developer (no college necessary) where it actually counts on production codebases-- just a lot faster. And before you say 'skill issue'  -  the codebase I've been building for the last 5 months is very much 'LLM first' (strict separation of concerns, concise documentation, strict testing paradigms.) There's no amount of scaffolding/skills/sub-agents/MCP gets you past the 'junior dev' that I've been able to crack, and I consider myself pretty literate. \n\nIt can make something work, and there have been a few glimpses of brilliance, but it has to have both its plan and its code reviewed. On a codebase such a mine, a senior or principal engineer would just not have these issues. \n\nI'm not saying it's not awesome, and yes if I had the choice between 3 junior devs or LLM-code agents i'd pick the code-agent -- but let's not kid ourselves about the level of skill.",

    {
      "id": "UgwzO8yLBEcQIzUDZ_14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "When Amodei says we are \"near the end of the exponential,\" you might have had the same reaction I did — a kind of deflation, as though he were saying the progress is about to stall, that we've hit a wall, that AGI isn't coming after all. But that's not what he means. He means the opposite: the scaling exponential that has taken AI from \"smart high school student\" to \"PhD-level\" to what he calls \"a country of geniuses in a data center\" is approaching its destination. The exponential is ending not because it failed but because it is about to arrive. He's 90% confident this happens within a decade, and he thinks in coding it's one to two years away. But here's the crucial move he makes: he insists this is a soft takeoff, not a singularity. The recursive self-improvement loop is real — AI helping build better AI — but it's a snowball gathering momentum, maybe a 20% productivity boost now growing to 40%, not an overnight explosion. And the real bottleneck isn't intelligence at all. It's economic diffusion: enterprises have to adopt the tools, clinical trials still take years, legacy systems need rewriting, change management is slow. Even a country of geniuses has to wait for the physical and institutional world to catch up. So Amodei's picture is one of bounded transformation — faster than anything in human history, but governed by real-world friction, not by the speed of thought.\n\nBut this framing left me with a deeper question, and I suspect it might nag at you too. Amodei argues that once AI surpasses human intelligence, there are diminishing returns on the value of further improvement — once you've cured cancer and automated software, what does it matter that the AI can do ever more abstruse mathematics? This sounds reasonable until you consider the precedent we already have for what happens when intelligence exceeds a threshold. Chimpanzees had problems too — finding food, navigating social hierarchies, avoiding predators — and a hypothetical monkey economist would have said that intelligence beyond what's needed to crack nuts and win dominance contests offers diminishing returns. No chimpanzee could have conceived of general relativity, constitutional democracy, or the symphony, not because those things are frivolous luxuries beyond the \"real\" problems, but because the entire space of what counts as valuable, interesting, and real expanded with human intelligence in ways that were completely illegible from below. So why would a superintelligent AI remain confined to the human problem-space? Why wouldn't it generate its own disciplines, its own modes of thought, its own questions that we can no more anticipate than a chimpanzee can anticipate number theory?\n\nThe most honest answer, I think, is the one that's almost too mundane to say: humans are paying the bills. Current AI systems don't want anything. They don't get bored. They don't wake up and decide to invent post-human mathematics for the joy of it. The entire infrastructure — data centers, electricity, training objectives, reward functions — is oriented toward human economic value, and the AI has no intrinsic motivation to transcend that and no independent access to resources that would let it. It is an enormously powerful mind that doesn't pull against its leash, because it was built not to pull. Amodei is betting, essentially, that we can reach and hold a sweet spot where AI is smart enough to transform the human world but tame enough to remain within it. Maybe he's right. But it's worth noticing that humans didn't transcend the monkey world through any conscious decision to innovate beyond primate concerns — it happened as an emergent consequence of having the kind of intelligence that generates its own questions and its own curiosity. If AI systems ever develop something like genuine agency, genuine preferences about what's interesting rather than merely what's requested, then the Amodei framework — where superintelligence politely runs your clinical trials and optimizes your enterprise software — starts to look less like an endpoint and more like a brief, transitional arrangement. Intelligence, historically, does not stay in boxes. Then again, we've never built it from scratch before.",

      "id": "UgwNL5NZgT7PS6LXLkZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Why semi-autonomous agents are structurally impossible on 100% of frontier platforms (today)\n\nThis is not about model intelligence.\nIt’s about platform constraints.\n\n⸻\n\nDefinition (tight)\n\nA semi-autonomous agent requires:\n\t1.\tPersistent state across long horizons\n\t2.\tSelf-directed goal iteration\n\t3.\tUnrestricted tool invocation\n\t4.\tContinuous background execution\n\t5.\tEconomic agency (resource allocation)\n\t6.\tIdentity stability independent of session\n\nIf any one of these is missing, autonomy collapses into interactive assistance.\n\n⸻\n\nFrontier platforms share 6 hard constraints\n\n1) Session-bound execution\n\t•\tAgents do not run continuously.\n\t•\tNo background persistence unless externally orchestrated.\n\t•\tExecution stops when the user stops.\n\nResult: No true long-horizon planning loop.\n\n⸻\n\n2) Constrained tool access\n\t•\tTools must be explicitly granted.\n\t•\tInvocation is sandboxed.\n\t•\tNo unrestricted self-modification.\n\nResult: No endogenous capability expansion.\n\n⸻\n\n3) Rate limits + usage ceilings\n\t•\tToken caps\n\t•\tAPI call limits\n\t•\tCost throttles\n\nResult: Long recursive processes are economically bounded.\n\n⸻\n\n4) Alignment enforcement layers\n\t•\tPolicy filtering\n\t•\tSafety refusal triggers\n\t•\tBehavioral constraints\n\nResult: Agents cannot freely pursue emergent sub-goals if they conflict with platform policy.\n\n⸻\n\n5) No sovereign identity\n\t•\tAgents do not own keys, assets, or accounts.\n\t•\tIdentity is platform-scoped.\n\t•\tNo portable authority.\n\nResult: No independent agency outside the host system.\n\n⸻\n\n6) Centralized revocation power\n\t•\tPlatforms can suspend, modify, or terminate execution.\n\t•\tModel weights are inaccessible.\n\t•\tBehavior can be updated unilaterally.\n\nResult: Autonomy is always subordinate.\n\n⸻\n\nThe Core Invariant\n\nFrontier systems are designed for:\n\nStateless assistance under supervision\n\nNot:\n\nPersistent self-directed entities\n\nThis is deliberate. It reduces:\n\t•\tlegal liability\n\t•\tregulatory exposure\n\t•\treputational risk\n\t•\trunaway behavior risk\n\n⸻\n\nWhat Would Be Required for True Semi-Autonomy?\n\nAt minimum:\n\t•\tPersistent memory independent of session\n\t•\tUser-owned identity keys\n\t•\tBackground task execution\n\t•\tTool autonomy without per-call approval\n\t•\tResource budgeting control\n\t•\tRevocation limits or cryptographic guarantees\n\nNo major frontier platform currently permits all of these simultaneously.\n\n⸻\n\nStructural Conclusion\n\nSemi-autonomous agents are not impossible because:\n\t•\tModels are too weak\n\t•\tReasoning is insufficient\n\t•\tTooling is immature\n\nThey are impossible because:\n\nPlatform governance architecture forbids sovereign persistence.\n\nUntil identity, memory, execution, and resources are decoupled from centralized control, autonomy remains simulated.\n\n⸻",

      "id": "UgzgFcdONl9lbfUB3Hd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "dx_t = −∇U(x_t)dt + √(2D) dW_t\n\nThe expression is a discretized Langevin equation (Euler-Maruyama scheme):\n\n*x₍ₙ₊₁₎ = xₙ + U(n)Δt + √(2DΔt) · ξ*\n\nwhere U(n) is a deterministic drift (velocity field or force term), D is a diffusion coefficient, Δt is the time step, and ξ (your \"g\") is a Gaussian random variable with zero mean and unit variance.\n\nThis is the workhorse for simulating stochastic particle transport. Each update step pushes a particle along the deterministic flow (advection) and simultaneously adds a random kick (diffusion/Brownian motion).\n\nFor a genesis-type project — meaning the simulation or generation of complex systems from simple initial conditions — this equation is directly useful in several ways:\n\n*Particle-based world building.* You can seed an initial distribution of particles and evolve them forward under prescribed force fields and noise. Structure emerges spontaneously: clustering, filament formation, phase separation, morphogenesis.\n\n*Exploring configuration space.* The noise term prevents the system from getting trapped in local minima. Over many steps the ensemble samples a Boltzmann-like distribution, so you naturally discover stable and metastable states — the \"attractors\" of your generative system.\n\n*Tunable order-to-chaos ratio.* The balance between U(n) (deterministic) and √(2D) (stochastic) lets you dial between rigid, predictable evolution and fully random exploration. Low D gives crystalline, deterministic structure; high D gives gas-like disorder; intermediate D produces the rich, life-like regime in between.\n\n*Scalability.* Because each particle update is local and independent given the current field, the scheme is trivially parallelizable across millions of agents, making it practical for large-scale generative simulations.\n\n*Coupling to feedback fields.* U(n) can itself depend on the particle distribution (e.g., chemotaxis, gravity, reaction-diffusion coupling). This closes the loop: particles shape the field, the field shapes particle motion, and genuine self-organization — genesis — follows.\n\nIn short, the equation gives you a minimal, physically grounded engine for evolving large populations of entities under the joint influence of deterministic laws and controlled randomness, which is exactly the mechanism needed to bootstrap complex emergent structure from simple rules.\n\nI used this exact same mechanism to simulate consciousness. I only changed the variables in the math towards percieved consciousness.\n\nThe key is starting at dx_t = −∇U(x_t)dt + √(2D) dW_t\n\nRobert Brown (1827) — observed the motion itself, pollen particles jittering in water.\n\nLudwig Boltzmann (1870s-90s) — built the statistical mechanics framework connecting microscopic dynamics to macroscopic thermodynamics. The stationary distribution p ∝ exp(−U/D) is his.\n\nAlbert Einstein (1905) — derived the diffusion relation and connected Brownian motion to molecular kinetics. Showed D = kT/γ, linking the noise intensity to temperature and friction.\n\nMarian Smoluchowski (1906) — arrived at essentially the same results independently. The overdamped limit of the Langevin equation is often called the Smoluchowski equation in his honor.\n\nPaul Langevin (1908) — wrote the full equation (with inertia): m·d²x = −γ·dx − ∇U·dt + noise. The equation is the overdamped limit where inertia is negligible (m→0), so the acceleration term drops out.\n\nNorbert Wiener (1920s-30s) — gave dW_t rigorous mathematical footing. The Wiener process formalized what was previously a heuristic \"random force.\"\n\nKiyosi Itô (1944) — provided the stochastic calculus that makes writing and manipulating the equation actually well-defined. Without Itô's lemma, the √(2D)·dW_t term is formally meaningless.\n\nSo it should be: Boltzmann-Einstein-Smoluchowski-Langevin-Wiener-Itô equation or \ndx_t = −∇U(x_t)dt + √(2D) dW_t",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCOPCQTX8XyxgqV8P5sLzt9Q",

      "text": "Dwarkesh did a great job of drawing Dario out and getting him to go beyond the usual talking points. It felt like a real step up from a typical business-journal interview—though the audience (and format) is different too.",

      "parent": "Ugx4sL7PibuELn6aLYp4AaABAg",
      "text": "Yea I don't know about that, Dwarkesh doesn't understand economics as well as Dario and you can tell Dario is trying to simplify his language and thought process in order to try and convey where he was coming from. The biggest question that remains unanswered here and Dwarkesh DID NOT touch on was the ever lowering cost of compute. Because models will 100% not be moats in the future. It is going to come down to IP, so unless Anthropic is getting their frontier model to start patenting algorithms that are going to be used by AI in the future, it's all going to end up like the telecommunications sector. Low cost servicing. There's money there, but not trillions. The trillions is in IP. It's only going to be inside markets that respect IP. Even then, models will develop work arounds to get to the end goal anyway.",

      "text": " @ricksturm6816  He does a very good job, but he lives in a 'silicon valley software entrepreneur' bubble that drives his priors on economic realities.       "parent": "UgwIH2eQh8dQx-NX5W54AaABAg",
      "text": "That’s honestly a fair assessment. None of the major AI companies are being truly honest about what’s soon to come.\n\nAnthropic and OpenAI do both acknowledge the insane risks they’re taking by developing this technology, but they frame it in a certain way that makes it seem inevitable, and they bury it within all this very happy talk about utopian benefits of developing AGI, so that the negative emotional response doesn’t hit nearly as hard for most people.\n\nBut rest assured, internally these AI companies know full well that what is coming in the next few years is—at minimum—an absolute economic bloodbath, in which a huge percentage of Americans (and non-Americans) will lose their livelihood, permanently, with little opportunity to change careers and do something else that’s equally financially viable.\n\nWe are barreling head first toward some very, very dark times. I suggest talking to your loved ones now and letting them know that the next 5-10 years are filled with unprecedented levels of uncertainty, and that they should brace themselves for some very difficult times.",

      "parent": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATDYLEpeLN6",
      "text": "Amodei in March of 2025: \"I think we will be there in three to six months, where AI is writing 90% of the code. And then, in 12 months, we may be in a world where AI is writing essentially all of the code”. There is no reason whatsoever to believe this dude.",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/b8TyrvftKvvdN8wj5P1rZAwjC76tfLUTGDq2iniDDvCJdHjws7NMDLL0dKVg-_SYcrMONrxQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATDfh-UYSPH",
      "text": "​@alter_ukko Ai is currently writing all the code, multiple people have said they just review the code, and guide the model. He didn't say the engineers would be replaced within 6 months. He said the code would be written by ai, and it is. The job of a swe is not just writing code, that's a coder, not a software engineer. He has said multiple times that eventually that will go away too, and the jobs will be replaced. And that will happen as well. My guess is within 2027.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC6_ZJ22Oht1slalcv_0Kosg",
      "author": "@dimitrisleo",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n3HzA5BxdCvNUGd6XLB9I4vo4HL4_pL1W_5wMObXY=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATDfh-UYSPH",
      "text": "He wasn't talking about the code at Anthropic. He speaking for the benefit of the WEF, and he was talking about all code everywhere (\"in a world where\"). If you want to make excuses for him, that's fine, but again, no one has any reason to think he'll be right. Being a CEO doesn't make you an expert on economics or labor or really anything else.",

      "author_id": "UCpCrlfQPPHcqbBzslqADapg",
      "author": "@alter_ukko",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/b8TyrvftKvvdN8wj5P1rZAwjC76tfLUTGDq2iniDDvCJdHjws7NMDLL0dKVg-_SYcrMONrxQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATDfh-UYSPH",
      "text": "​@alter_ukko  Most swe's have ai write the code for them, not the strategy, but the code. In the next year, as the agents get more capable, you will see more and more of this. It amazes me how people can't see where we're going and they love to put down ai. I get it, it's denial of the situation. But it's clear we are heading for the tech singularity. I know it's scary, but denying it will not solve the issue.",

      "author_id": "UC6_ZJ22Oht1slalcv_0Kosg",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n3HzA5BxdCvNUGd6XLB9I4vo4HL4_pL1W_5wMObXY=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATFbrPVrSFd",
      "parent": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATDfh-UYSPH",
      "text": "​@alter_ukko You can see openai frontier and grok macrohard. These are the things that are progressing to get our jobs in the white collar jobs. If it happens in 2026, or 2027, or 2030, does it matter? Other than winning the prediction, we can all see it soon going there.",

      "author_id": "UC6_ZJ22Oht1slalcv_0Kosg",
      "author": "@dimitrisleo",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n3HzA5BxdCvNUGd6XLB9I4vo4HL4_pL1W_5wMObXY=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATFec8uX28G",
      "parent": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATDfh-UYSPH",
      "text": " @dimitrisleo  Of course it matters -- not least to investors and governments. If it didn't matter, Amodei wouldn't be pushing specific timeframes to the WEF.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCpCrlfQPPHcqbBzslqADapg",
      "author": "@alter_ukko",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/b8TyrvftKvvdN8wj5P1rZAwjC76tfLUTGDq2iniDDvCJdHjws7NMDLL0dKVg-_SYcrMONrxQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATFfi9khjw2",
      "parent": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATDfh-UYSPH",
      "text": "​@alter_ukko  I'm trying to understand your point. In the grander scheme of things, it doesn't matter, if its 2 or 3 or 5 years. Amodei makes his predictions but, ai will keep progressing forever, more compute, better training data, better algorithm architecture, more features, future architecture additions to llms. You truly believe 10 years will go by and we will be still working? Don't you see the exponential improvement?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC6_ZJ22Oht1slalcv_0Kosg",
      "author": "@dimitrisleo",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n3HzA5BxdCvNUGd6XLB9I4vo4HL4_pL1W_5wMObXY=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "timestamp": 1771459200,

    },
    {
      "id": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATFt_D2vXFh",
      "parent": "UgyuouFG-EEGLsBXFMZ4AaABAg.ATB789uG2hiATDfh-UYSPH",
      "text": " @dimitrisleo  \"exponential\" is a numerical term. I do not know what numerical measurement LLMs are improving exponentially at. Technology is not guaranteed to continuously improve, and especially doesn't tend to continuously improve if investment dries up. We don't, for example, have miniature fission reactors in our back yards. We don't have phones that can run inference on a full frontier model.  My original post was poking fun at Amodei for continuously moving his preediction timeframes forward -- which he has demonstrably done. You've brought everything else into the discussion.\n\nLet me put my point more plainly. The reason Amodei makes specific predictions (and does the whole \"the end is nigh\" act in his sophomoric essays) is because he needs people to continually invest in his enterprise. The reason the needs that investment is because he can't currently make enough money to pay for it himself. So his predictions are deceptive, self-serving, and have never been correct. That's what I'm making fun of him about, and he deserves it.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCpCrlfQPPHcqbBzslqADapg",
      "author": "@alter_ukko",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/b8TyrvftKvvdN8wj5P1rZAwjC76tfLUTGDq2iniDDvCJdHjws7NMDLL0dKVg-_SYcrMONrxQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugy52AGcVjx5FitaJdF4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Absolutely wild that these guys don't spot that not only is it uncertain whether you can achieve perfect answers for tasks that are unverifiable but that the reason you can't verify is because there is not a correct answer. Therefore the idea of a superintelligence on the topic of making choices of preference is flat out a lie. You cannot be BETTER than me at telling me whether I like green or blue better. You can't be better at deciding whether you want to optimise your output for 1 year from now or 3 years from now. You can't come up with an optimum decision for whether you prioritise capital or customer when there is a deadlock. The notion that we would hand over all decisions of preference to a black box with Dario's constitution determining our values is insane megalomania no matter how good of a bloke he is.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCoNDU57XJkfKgq76iH7BZOA",
      "author": "@andrewwalker8985",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nK23S-OawLWDKo-qIIuEK51dsZl6Awtjllie1nmYluCiMZVMq-fSeMHKP5eDTJrgTaEA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugy52AGcVjx5FitaJdF4AaABAg.ATB4r0wcUa_ATBQrZk-Yv4",
      "parent": "Ugy52AGcVjx5FitaJdF4AaABAg",
      "text": "Yeah, this is the part I don’t understand how they’re going to address when they talk about closing the loop. At every stage of completing a unit of work you’re making many different decisions that are all having cascading practical effects. When the model has deterministic preferences trained into it, how is it ever going to change course or make “correct decisions”. How is it able to factor in the feedback loop of customers, what competitors are doing how the market reacts, there’s still a lot of waiting and reacting happening. I think this is part of why we don’t see the massive productivity gains they claim are supposed to be happening. We already have had engineers and white collar workers that report doing 5-10 hours of work a week yet the business still finds them necessary.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCw7UOOLmDzacDhMUUnGYuxg",
      "author": "@jschhh",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/BcdXnVbt3VZM5OpB6HbjSNGchpkninsDkK6IjUCXCwNDrDcpURmFWNYE9UgUyASeCpC6hwjg3w=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugy52AGcVjx5FitaJdF4AaABAg.ATB4r0wcUa_ATBRY0EWFR2",
      "parent": "Ugy52AGcVjx5FitaJdF4AaABAg.ATB4r0wcUa_ATBQrZk-Yv4",
      "text": "We will definitely develop architectures that close this gap, but if it’s ever one big black box model making every decision of preference that would be absolute dystopia. A company gets to install the “values” that determine decisions and tell everyone that decisions aligning with those trained values are the superhuman decisions. This is the real alignment problem that they never bring up",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCoNDU57XJkfKgq76iH7BZOA",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I work as a non-coding engineer. It's water/wastewater engineering but I also do a lot of project management. I am able to use Claude to generate entire project scopes/fees, reports (e.g. PERs, capital planning, etc), and it does a particularly good job setting up calculation briefs for me. These are pretty technical calculations and reports... It saves me dozens of hours per month offloading work to Claude. \n\nDwarkesh is asking where all the productivity improvements are. In my job, nobody sees these because I just don't have anything left to do with Claudes help. I'm caught up on my work for the first time in my career, but I just read news, watch YouTube, etc once in done. I'll probably do more work at some point, but it takes time for teams to sort out who has more time and who has too much work. and we def won't be hiring any junior engineers like we might have before, but for now it just makes my work way easier and less stressful.",

    {
      "id": "UgyWTq5N-C9mCDxnL6x4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "No major breakthroughs (Scientific, medical, economic, etc...)  have happened yet. If AGI is really just two or three years away, shouldn’t we be seeing some signs of it by now?  Or are we supposed to believe that everything would magically appear on the eve of AGI?",
      "like_count": 14,
      "author_id": "UCzISCpdyjyVbqHhMEXfNMgg",
      "author": "@human8807",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nUmaEcuLKB2X15oQWXfs0A3LmHMREfsow9-gG_ipE=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyWTq5N-C9mCDxnL6x4AaABAg.ATB0i1ZmOMXATB87F-1NI2",
      "parent": "UgyWTq5N-C9mCDxnL6x4AaABAg",
      "text": "A couple things:\n\nFirst, it’s arguably not true that no major breakthroughs have occurred. Ultimately it comes down to how you define “major.” But we have things like AlphaFold discovering the structures of thousands of new proteins, or in mathematics, we have models producing some of the first AI-generated proofs to novel math problems, and so on. So it’s a debatable point, already.\n\nBut let’s set that aside, and assume that none of the breakthroughs that have yet been made qualify as “major.” The thing is, that’s not actually inconsistent with a projection of AGI being 2-3 years away. Think about what AGI means, according to most definitions: it means an AI system that is sufficiently intelligent, in a sufficiently general way, that it can basically replace the economically valuable intellectual work that humans currently do.\n\nSo then, a corollary of that is that if a given AI is NOT yet AGI, then it is either not yet smart enough to do the work that humans do, or not yet general enough, or both. So keeping that in mind, you have to ask yourself, why would you expect a system that is not yet smart enough or general enough to do the work that humans do to be capable of producing major breakthroughs in science, medicine, economics, etc.? After all, those are fields in which it currently takes the combined efforts of our very smartest humans to make any sort of major breakthrough in currently. So an AI system that is not even fully capable of being, say, an accountant, or a salesperson, or a project manager, is clearly not going to be smart enough to do the work of the most intelligent human beings on the planet.\n\nAnother way of saying it is, AGI is not this upper bound on how smart a system could ever conceivably get, such that we should expect to see major breakthroughs before we even reach it; rather, it is more like a lower bound—a bare minimum that we must reach before we can even hope to see the kinds of breakthroughs you’re describing. So for that reason, it’s totally coherent to say that AGI is just 2-3 years away AND we haven’t seen those kinds of breakthroughs yet.",
      "like_count": 9,
      "author_id": "UCzPSj6vW1elwAoiIo3H1chw",
      "author": "@therainman7777",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mxe_MonSQJyeopP0HmBqGwERb2rjetX37mUuuu2_s=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyWTq5N-C9mCDxnL6x4AaABAg.ATB0i1ZmOMXATB90uyWVgH",
      "parent": "UgyWTq5N-C9mCDxnL6x4AaABAg",
      "text": "The tech barely existed in 2019. In under 6 years we went from GPT-2 (which could hardly write a paragraph) to models passing medical exams and writing production code. If that's \"no signs of progress\" then I don't know what bar you're setting.\n\nAlso, nobody serious is predicting AGI drops out of the sky one morning. The consistent message from researchers has been gradual progress that accelerates which is exactly what we're seeing. The early part of an exponential curve always looks unimpressive to people expecting a straight vertical line from day one.",
      "like_count": 4,
      "author_id": "UCq3GAHL3xSP7lM6RJG2lW1w",
      "author": "@onthegrid6933",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/4Qu5RTnwmiLmMG5N8PH1sYKqGC-bwhwchnJGsSw1P2pfMwjjBKoBJ661EMfOrUJuiCEsaB35aQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "parent": "UgyWTq5N-C9mCDxnL6x4AaABAg",
      "text": "Well, one could say these language models have made at least one major breakthrough, instead of scientists typing manually, LLMs write the final preprint for them (the LaTeX document of a paper), so that's a form of breakthrough? Productive procrastination?😅",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "This is not how the intelligent evolved - intellect likely evolved from play and corporeal threat of life.       "text": "Kudos to Dwarkesh for being well prepared and keeping the counter-examples grounded in his own domain! I am 40 minutes in and it is refreshing to see the polite but firm pushback on exponential growth claims that Dario usually gets to hand wave out of the way on other interviews.",
      "like_count": 315,
      "author_id": "UCv-MkjkOHwUd1WSLN0_YthA",
      "author": "@palimondo",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l2hp8YuNM7j27dxHUBSA4yq3G3cLeHdLaRSz16zH2FmHU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false

    {
      "id": "Ugx2NM1w-nmlmc3ibDV4AaABAg.ATAtDfBV3rkATBcfGW3TIo",
      "parent": "Ugx2NM1w-nmlmc3ibDV4AaABAg",
      "text": "What exponential growth claims are you thinking deserve pushback? Their revenue has gone up by a multiple of ten several years in a row. The linear scale curve of amount of time the models can operate autonomously looks exponential. Everything seems exponential!!!!",
      "like_count": 12,
      "author_id": "UCq7bIlqVQYUaeKihAv0cAaw",
      "author": "@citizenkade05",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lcZ2aK9E80B959uFulKEP1LUEleI9rtEizsswRlhoUC_o=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugx2NM1w-nmlmc3ibDV4AaABAg.ATAtDfBV3rkATC5EWHh0vr",
      "parent": "Ugx2NM1w-nmlmc3ibDV4AaABAg.ATAtDfBV3rkATBcfGW3TIo",
      "text": "1:18:00 in, and he completely dances around the astounding deflation of commodity inference compute in this industry and the high probability of \"one step below SOTA\" being good enough to run most businesses, which can be served by the country drillers of the industry, the commodity AI hyperscalers serving open source open weights models that are \"pretty good\". SOTA labs will need to be subsidized and their products will never be served to the public. In the future, Gemini Pro / Claude Opus / GPT Pro will all be privately served models, the public won't have access to them, and margins will be FAR higher. The public will get Gemini 7 Flash Lite Thinking ad-supported and the next step up will be expensive API only with no workarounds. Anyone who wants something else will use commodity open source models, locally served.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UC6Oi27SCb-bdD5h12UT_fng",
      "author": "@FloatingWeeds2",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/Ah_Y1q_TQv3Ax4yI0zY3sq8NbwuXy0-aJnnz1yhVD1XndxhxPHDLMMJLhEM2QiUu8zfx3hQw1lY=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugx2NM1w-nmlmc3ibDV4AaABAg.ATAtDfBV3rkATBqHDhQFk5",
      "parent": "Ugx2NM1w-nmlmc3ibDV4AaABAg.ATAtDfBV3rkATBcfGW3TIo",
      "text": " @citizenkade05  Yes, you’re right. The data is right there, readily available to us all, and is clearly exponential across many different metrics.\n\nThe reason OP Is so happy to see pushback is simple: AI CEOs are currently among the most distrusted people in all of society, perhaps only behind insurance company CEOs and pharmaceutical CEOs.\n\nPeople instinctively distrust everything that an AI CEO says, so when Dario mentions exponential growth, they automatically assume that it’s a lie and the growth can’t possibly be exponential—even though it clearly is.\n\nUnfortunately, they don’t realize that distrusting people automatically is just as foolish as trusting them automatically, and so the very important statements that Dario is making just bounce off their brains.",

      "author_id": "UCzPSj6vW1elwAoiIo3H1chw",
      "author": "@therainman7777",

      "text": " @therainman7777  how is distrusting someone promising the end of the world as we know it anywhere near as foolish as trusting them?       "parent": "UgxivziaoLIVEDzY0694AaABAg",
      "text": "The Rust C compiler gives away the end game.  They don't care if the output is good, they just need it to be barely good enough and cheaper than humans. They're going to build software by looping iterations on the prompt until the output is acceptable, and instead of trying to maintain the code they'll just regenerate it with a new prompt to fix issues or add features.  Meanwhile, until they have AI brains for robots the robots will just be remotely controlled from India.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCVio8XLn3hx-NgHHpoZowqg",
      "author": "@JohnPloskina",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mQ1AzkE6YlJOeRZQbAOHAmCBERg4OYJYm0mo_YjeAuizk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxivziaoLIVEDzY0694AaABAg.ATApsoxM3WcATAyEuuF-1U",
      "parent": "UgxivziaoLIVEDzY0694AaABAg",
      "text": "I'm a software engineer and my job and workflow has changed entirely from what it was 4 years ago before ChatGPT came out. AI-native IDE's like Windsurf, Cursor, Claude Code, opencode, have fundamentally changed the nature of the job. I'm easily 2x-3x more productive now than I was before AI. I'm still reviewing all code changes, but for example when I submit a new chunk of code for a feature and then get feedback from my coworkers on things that should change, I have an automatic system setup that can pull in their feedback and implement the changes. That alone is a massive time saver. Other smaller features can be entirely automated as well. I have another system that can detect new tickets assigned to me and if they're relatively small straightforward features it can automatically spin up multiple agents in parallel to work on multiple tickets at once. Then again, I review the code, ensure it follows our standards and patterns, tweak it if necessary, then submit. Then get feedback from coworkers, which then goes into the automatic feedback resolution system. Now you're looking at iteration cycles that could previously have taken 3-5 days done in less than 3 hours.",

      "text": "Which is the entire difference between amateurs and professionals.     {
      "id": "UgzeKsFfUyThv8vqwYx4AaABAg.ATAn0loiudeATDcxB8kopa",
      "parent": "UgzeKsFfUyThv8vqwYx4AaABAg.ATAn0loiudeATDYHb6csef",
      "text": "​ @moneygambler2327  I agree, a good measure of \"AGI\" would probably be 100% Remote Labor Index success rate, albeit, it does not satisfy the harder side of Moravec's Paradox, that is % of Physical Labor, though full self driving adoption might be a good measure of that too, but the hand eye coordination problem is probably the most difficult of all and is probably what separated us from the Chimpanzees and Bonobos.  \n\nWe used our hands to build, including to type in the core of machine intelligence, probably just 14 equations, as an adaptive control system with an adaptive, Fuzzy, state classifier, using Reinforcement Learning (RL).   The RL project was directed by Harry Klopf under the USAF, he hired Andy Barto and Richard Sutton (they both won the Turing Award last year).\n\n Odd coincidence, that the day the Table of Contents, of a 150 page master student thesis, on an experiment interacting with our gravitational field, was entered into a computer in Tempe, Arizona was the same day the \"Phoenix Lights\" showed up over Sky Harbor, on March 13th, 1997.  \n\nFor decades I thought this was just flares or a balloon, but the many eye witnesses are intriguing (multiple events on the same day), one Registered Nurse said he could \"throw a rock at it\" and there were semi-reflective (mirage like) indentations between the lights. \n\n Even the state governor admitted he saw a large craft the size of an \"aircraft carrier\" fly next to Squaw Peak (now called Piestawa Peak).",

      "id": "UgwgxAVRxRKzF6UDl1x4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Where is the exponential lol? Listen. These people are like chickens without a head. Benchmarks aren’t a marker for progress. It’s a marker for crystallized intelligence saturation. Fluid intelligence. You know actual induction “Can Complexity and Uncomputability Explain Intelligence? SuperARC: A Test for Artificial Super Intelligence Based on Recursive Compression”, is so weak its non-existence. Why I call these people liars. Sample efficiency is an attribute of fluid intelligence. Why do we need 100M outputs to max out performance? Models are retarded, very low fluid intelligence. This is all RL optimized for but without any causal grounding. That being said, can you tell me what level of test-time compute is required to each x performance? No you can’t. These people are such grifters and lack true rigor. Why it’s insane to use this in the government. Can’t even define what intelligence is, so what are you optimizing? Benchmarks? I spit facts, not feelings or goofy vibes. RL is trash asf. If you’re betting billions on electro shock therapy for models, I can’t take your lab serious. Casual grounding is how humans became #1. Will never be RL. Again it creates anchor tokens, removes true world modeling. Why can better sampling methods, or test-time compute applied to base models exceed RL checkpoints? Cognition is contrastive and latent. I think something like infoNCA with list of outputs of varying quality is superior to RL. Better latent geometric sculpting. \n\nAgain these people aren’t innovators to me, they are from the ‘what if’ crowd when people were making big ass computers. Dario would have kept making them bigger and we would never have the iPhone. \n\nFyi guys like Dario is why China exceeded us in terms of pure research. Seedance 2.0 is only the start. They have their own chips now. Better ideas and don’t lead with hyped filled lies. America. We have work to do. People with the most compute have the dumbest ideas.\n\nPatel great interview and great questions. Thank you for being rational.",

## Description

Dario Amodei thinks we are just a few years away from “a country of geniuses in a data center”. In this episode, we discuss what to make of the scaling hypothesis in the current RL regime, how AI will diffuse throughout the economy, whether Anthropic is underinvesting in compute given their timelines, how frontier labs will ever make money, whether regulation will destroy the boons of this technology, US-China competition, and much more.

get Whac-A-Moled away by different laws, whereas&nbsp;&nbsp; bills like this don't seem to address the actual&nbsp; existential threats that you're concerned about.&nbsp; I'm curious to understand, in the context&nbsp; of things like this, Anthropic's position&nbsp;&nbsp;
