Yeah, they are quite large context. The problem is, what to put, and does the model remember everything? Maybe it does. I agree on that. It takes that as a human, on-the-go learning, and has everything in that 1 million context in the model's context.
> Still, when you're working, even as an SDE, there are 5 code bases involved. There would be a time when a senior engineer would have told you, "We have to do this this way because there is something on that code base that works like this, and if we do it this way, that would benefit us, or if we do not, this would cost us something." This happens all the time, but this is not the one million moving window. When I am working in SDE, working on some new feature, it's not like that one million context before this point of time contains all these things that would help me in designing the architecture. If the last 1M words before that time would contain everything needed than it would work . The human brain just instantly searches the needed information at that point of time. This is the basic magic that human brain has. What Claude Code, etc., does is it grabs, search, etc tool calls. The human brain doesn't search; it directly reaches that point when someone told something related to what I am doing right now. This is not a one million moving context window where, from this point of time, the last 1 million tokens consist of all of that critical information. > Don't get me wrong, I assume Dario Amodei is a very smart person, smarter than me. But I did some googling and I can't find anything that suggests he himself has any SWE experience so I'm not sure he has much experience to make such bold claims that he does. He is also a CEO and CEO's have a duty to public relations and hyping their company and product 24/7 for their shareholders, so you simply cannot believe them outright.
> 
> Anthropic has paraded that they have written a C compiler entirely with AI which sounds super impressive until you engage your brain for a second and realize, a c compiler (if not multiple was certainly part of it's training data, and the resulting c compiler it made was inarguably worse than compilers already out there and that it took an intense amount of structure and defined testing and hand holding to make it happen. "Woo, look at this, your jobs are over because we were able to make it do a thing that has already existed for 50 years"
> 
> Cursor also recently supposedly made a whole browser with only a team of agents, except, it was barely a browser, couldn't even run browser tests to see how much of the standard it covers and was FULL of literally stolen code, right from Ladybird.
> 
> This reveals the problem which is obvious to anyone who has a middling understanding of how LLMs work. They don't create, they can only infer based on training data weights and context. There are not many browsers and basically one in Rust so when it had to build one in Rust, it had no choice but to steal code because it cannot, *actually*, create.
> 
> What  LLM's are FANTASTIC for is, SWE's steal code all the time already. LLM's are just better at it. Even when making something brand new, a huge chunk of the code is going to be incredibly similar to something that has existed before. That's why stackoverflow was so successful for so long, it was a place to grab useful proven snippets of functionality that SWE's could plug together like lego to build things. In many automation tasks, there might be absolutely nothing unique about the task and an LLM can easily do it flawlessly. However, if you are actually innovating or doing something new, you will find out how actually completely unusable LLM's become in that space. What I'm finding out is that so many SWEs do not work with innovate new code... which is why I think so many people get duped into thinking LLM's are capable of more than they are

> Second, all the SOTA models are domain specialized. The models that are good at Go can't play chess; the models that are good at manipulating languages can't play Go. They don't generalize out of distribution. So there goes the "G". 
> They do something that appears to be reasoning but in fact is not reasoning at all as a couple of published papers have shown in recent months(which is totally unsurprising if one knows the inner work of those models). 
> 
> Most importantly, humans don't function by "reasoning" most of the time. AND reasoning is not just a set of logical steps to reach an answer. If it were, philosophers who use logic would all come to the same conclusion.
>  The right hemisphere is far more important than the left hemisphere. It's how people understand maths, physics and all the other complex subjects on the intuitive level yet the tech bros have put zero effort into understanding & modeling how the right hemisphere works with the left hemisphere to achieve genuine understanding. > I could go on but the missing pieces for AGI is far too many for this tiny space to contain.

> I am coming from this from a historiographical perspective more than anything, but it seems like Dario is attempting to launder the Fukayamaist position that representative democracy and capitalism are forever interlocked as the best combination of political and economic organisation, while at the same time saying that capitalism will end and this new economic system will replace it but it'll retain liberalist principles just because... he likes them i guess? The last time this happened, when capitalism was first attempted in the Netherlands and England in the mid 1600s, it was followed not by an age of widespread social upheaval and liberation, but by the literal Age of Absolutism, where monarchs across europe quite literally consolidated absolute power, where colossal nation-states were directed under the power of one person, ending in the most powerful form of authoritarianism ever attempted in the history of humanity. It was the overthrow of this horrifically repressive political system during the age of revolutions that lead to capitalism becoming the dominant form of economic organisation, not the other way around. Unless you can give some sort of evidence that this time it's going to be magically different (despite the overwhelming rise of anti-democratic hypernationalism in every single representative democracy on the face of the earth right now implying the exact opposite), I think that the rise of AI is simply going to allow the hyper-rich countries that invent it to become just that: even more fantastically wealthy, and nothing more. China right now is living proof that you don't need civil liberties to have a healthy, fast growing, extremely productive economy just as capable of making the line go up as anywhere else. In my opinion, societies that are unable to manage the large wealth inequalities that disruptive technologies and hyper-productive economic systems naturally create are the ones that do not survive, because that's exactly what happened last time, and the time before that, and the time before that.

### Comment 1873
- comment_id: UgwzO8yLBEcQIzUDZ_14AaABAg
- parent_id: root
- author: @brian.edwards

> When Amodei says we are "near the end of the exponential," you might have had the same reaction I did — a kind of deflation, as though he were saying the progress is about to stall, that we've hit a wall, that AGI isn't coming after all. But that's not what he means. He means the opposite: the scaling exponential that has taken AI from "smart high school student" to "PhD-level" to what he calls "a country of geniuses in a data center" is approaching its destination. The exponential is ending not because it failed but because it is about to arrive. He's 90% confident this happens within a decade, and he thinks in coding it's one to two years away. But here's the crucial move he makes: he insists this is a soft takeoff, not a singularity. The recursive self-improvement loop is real — AI helping build better AI — but it's a snowball gathering momentum, maybe a 20% productivity boost now growing to 40%, not an overnight explosion. And the real bottleneck isn't intelligence at all. It's economic diffusion: enterprises have to adopt the tools, clinical trials still take years, legacy systems need rewriting, change management is slow. Even a country of geniuses has to wait for the physical and institutional world to catch up. So Amodei's picture is one of bounded transformation — faster than anything in human history, but governed by real-world friction, not by the speed of thought.
> 
> But this framing left me with a deeper question, and I suspect it might nag at you too. Amodei argues that once AI surpasses human intelligence, there are diminishing returns on the value of further improvement — once you've cured cancer and automated software, what does it matter that the AI can do ever more abstruse mathematics? This sounds reasonable until you consider the precedent we already have for what happens when intelligence exceeds a threshold. Chimpanzees had problems too — finding food, navigating social hierarchies, avoiding predators — and a hypothetical monkey economist would have said that intelligence beyond what's needed to crack nuts and win dominance contests offers diminishing returns. No chimpanzee could have conceived of general relativity, constitutional democracy, or the symphony, not because those things are frivolous luxuries beyond the "real" problems, but because the entire space of what counts as valuable, interesting, and real expanded with human intelligence in ways that were completely illegible from below. So why would a superintelligent AI remain confined to the human problem-space? Why wouldn't it generate its own disciplines, its own modes of thought, its own questions that we can no more anticipate than a chimpanzee can anticipate number theory?
> 
> The most honest answer, I think, is the one that's almost too mundane to say: humans are paying the bills. Current AI systems don't want anything. They don't get bored. They don't wake up and decide to invent post-human mathematics for the joy of it. The entire infrastructure — data centers, electricity, training objectives, reward functions — is oriented toward human economic value, and the AI has no intrinsic motivation to transcend that and no independent access to resources that would let it. It is an enormously powerful mind that doesn't pull against its leash, because it was built not to pull. Amodei is betting, essentially, that we can reach and hold a sweet spot where AI is smart enough to transform the human world but tame enough to remain within it. Maybe he's right. But it's worth noticing that humans didn't transcend the monkey world through any conscious decision to innovate beyond primate concerns — it happened as an emergent consequence of having the kind of intelligence that generates its own questions and its own curiosity. If AI systems ever develop something like genuine agency, genuine preferences about what's interesting rather than merely what's requested, then the Amodei framework — where superintelligence politely runs your clinical trials and optimizes your enterprise software — starts to look less like an endpoint and more like a brief, transitional arrangement. Intelligence, historically, does not stay in boxes. Then again, we've never built it from scratch before.

> Why semi-autonomous agents are structurally impossible on 100% of frontier platforms (today)
> 
> This is not about model intelligence.
> It’s about platform constraints.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> Definition (tight)
> 
> A semi-autonomous agent requires:
> 	1.	Persistent state across long horizons
> 	2.	Self-directed goal iteration
> 	3.	Unrestricted tool invocation
> 	4.	Continuous background execution
> 	5.	Economic agency (resource allocation)
> 	6.	Identity stability independent of session
> 
> If any one of these is missing, autonomy collapses into interactive assistance.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> Frontier platforms share 6 hard constraints
> 
> 1) Session-bound execution
> 	•	Agents do not run continuously.
> 	•	No background persistence unless externally orchestrated.
> 	•	Execution stops when the user stops.
> 
> Result: No true long-horizon planning loop.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> 2) Constrained tool access
> 	•	Tools must be explicitly granted.
> 	•	Invocation is sandboxed.
> 	•	No unrestricted self-modification.
> 
> Result: No endogenous capability expansion.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> 3) Rate limits + usage ceilings
> 	•	Token caps
> 	•	API call limits
> 	•	Cost throttles
> 
> Result: Long recursive processes are economically bounded.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> 4) Alignment enforcement layers
> 	•	Policy filtering
> 	•	Safety refusal triggers
> 	•	Behavioral constraints
> 
> Result: Agents cannot freely pursue emergent sub-goals if they conflict with platform policy.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> 5) No sovereign identity
> 	•	Agents do not own keys, assets, or accounts.
> 	•	Identity is platform-scoped.
> 	•	No portable authority.
> 
> Result: No independent agency outside the host system.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> 6) Centralized revocation power
> 	•	Platforms can suspend, modify, or terminate execution.
> 	•	Model weights are inaccessible.
> 	•	Behavior can be updated unilaterally.
> 
> Result: Autonomy is always subordinate.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> The Core Invariant
> 
> Frontier systems are designed for:
> 
> Stateless assistance under supervision
> 
> Not:
> 
> Persistent self-directed entities
> 
> This is deliberate. It reduces:
> 	•	legal liability
> 	•	regulatory exposure
> 	•	reputational risk
> 	•	runaway behavior risk
> 
> ⸻
> 
> What Would Be Required for True Semi-Autonomy?
> 
> At minimum:
> 	•	Persistent memory independent of session
> 	•	User-owned identity keys
> 	•	Background task execution
> 	•	Tool autonomy without per-call approval
> 	•	Resource budgeting control
> 	•	Revocation limits or cryptographic guarantees
> 
> No major frontier platform currently permits all of these simultaneously.
> 
> ⸻
> 
> Structural Conclusion
> 
> Semi-autonomous agents are not impossible because:
> 	•	Models are too weak
> 	•	Reasoning is insufficient
> 	•	Tooling is immature
> 
> They are impossible because:
> 
> Platform governance architecture forbids sovereign persistence.
> 
> Until identity, memory, execution, and resources are decoupled from centralized control, autonomy remains simulated.
> 
> ⸻

> dx_t = −∇U(x_t)dt + √(2D) dW_t
> 
> The expression is a discretized Langevin equation (Euler-Maruyama scheme):
> 
> *x₍ₙ₊₁₎ = xₙ + U(n)Δt + √(2DΔt) · ξ*
> 
> where U(n) is a deterministic drift (velocity field or force term), D is a diffusion coefficient, Δt is the time step, and ξ (your "g") is a Gaussian random variable with zero mean and unit variance.
> 
> This is the workhorse for simulating stochastic particle transport. Each update step pushes a particle along the deterministic flow (advection) and simultaneously adds a random kick (diffusion/Brownian motion).
> 
> For a genesis-type project — meaning the simulation or generation of complex systems from simple initial conditions — this equation is directly useful in several ways:
> 
> *Particle-based world building.* You can seed an initial distribution of particles and evolve them forward under prescribed force fields and noise. Structure emerges spontaneously: clustering, filament formation, phase separation, morphogenesis.
> 
> *Exploring configuration space.* The noise term prevents the system from getting trapped in local minima. Over many steps the ensemble samples a Boltzmann-like distribution, so you naturally discover stable and metastable states — the "attractors" of your generative system.
> 
> *Tunable order-to-chaos ratio.* The balance between U(n) (deterministic) and √(2D) (stochastic) lets you dial between rigid, predictable evolution and fully random exploration. Low D gives crystalline, deterministic structure; high D gives gas-like disorder; intermediate D produces the rich, life-like regime in between.
> 
> *Scalability.* Because each particle update is local and independent given the current field, the scheme is trivially parallelizable across millions of agents, making it practical for large-scale generative simulations.
> 
> *Coupling to feedback fields.* U(n) can itself depend on the particle distribution (e.g., chemotaxis, gravity, reaction-diffusion coupling). This closes the loop: particles shape the field, the field shapes particle motion, and genuine self-organization — genesis — follows.
> 
> In short, the equation gives you a minimal, physically grounded engine for evolving large populations of entities under the joint influence of deterministic laws and controlled randomness, which is exactly the mechanism needed to bootstrap complex emergent structure from simple rules.
> 
> I used this exact same mechanism to simulate consciousness. I only changed the variables in the math towards percieved consciousness.
> 
> The key is starting at dx_t = −∇U(x_t)dt + √(2D) dW_t
> 
> Robert Brown (1827) — observed the motion itself, pollen particles jittering in water.
> 
> Ludwig Boltzmann (1870s-90s) — built the statistical mechanics framework connecting microscopic dynamics to macroscopic thermodynamics. The stationary distribution p ∝ exp(−U/D) is his.
> 
> Albert Einstein (1905) — derived the diffusion relation and connected Brownian motion to molecular kinetics. Showed D = kT/γ, linking the noise intensity to temperature and friction.
> 
> Marian Smoluchowski (1906) — arrived at essentially the same results independently. The overdamped limit of the Langevin equation is often called the Smoluchowski equation in his honor.
> 
> Paul Langevin (1908) — wrote the full equation (with inertia): m·d²x = −γ·dx − ∇U·dt + noise. The equation is the overdamped limit where inertia is negligible (m→0), so the acceleration term drops out.
> 
> Norbert Wiener (1920s-30s) — gave dW_t rigorous mathematical footing. The Wiener process formalized what was previously a heuristic "random force."
> 
> Kiyosi Itô (1944) — provided the stochastic calculus that makes writing and manipulating the equation actually well-defined. Without Itô's lemma, the √(2D)·dW_t term is formally meaningless.
> 
> So it should be: Boltzmann-Einstein-Smoluchowski-Langevin-Wiener-Itô equation or 
> dx_t = −∇U(x_t)dt + √(2D) dW_t

### Comment 2108
- comment_id: UgyWTq5N-C9mCDxnL6x4AaABAg.ATB0i1ZmOMXATB87F-1NI2
- parent_id: UgyWTq5N-C9mCDxnL6x4AaABAg
- author: @therainman7777
- author_id: UCzPSj6vW1elwAoiIo3H1chw
- published_at: 2026-02-19T00:00:00.000Z
- like_count: 9
- is_favorited: false
- author_is_uploader: false

> A couple things:
> 
> First, it’s arguably not true that no major breakthroughs have occurred. Ultimately it comes down to how you define “major.” But we have things like AlphaFold discovering the structures of thousands of new proteins, or in mathematics, we have models producing some of the first AI-generated proofs to novel math problems, and so on. So it’s a debatable point, already.
> 
> But let’s set that aside, and assume that none of the breakthroughs that have yet been made qualify as “major.” The thing is, that’s not actually inconsistent with a projection of AGI being 2-3 years away. Think about what AGI means, according to most definitions: it means an AI system that is sufficiently intelligent, in a sufficiently general way, that it can basically replace the economically valuable intellectual work that humans currently do.
> 
> So then, a corollary of that is that if a given AI is NOT yet AGI, then it is either not yet smart enough to do the work that humans do, or not yet general enough, or both. So keeping that in mind, you have to ask yourself, why would you expect a system that is not yet smart enough or general enough to do the work that humans do to be capable of producing major breakthroughs in science, medicine, economics, etc.? After all, those are fields in which it currently takes the combined efforts of our very smartest humans to make any sort of major breakthrough in currently. So an AI system that is not even fully capable of being, say, an accountant, or a salesperson, or a project manager, is clearly not going to be smart enough to do the work of the most intelligent human beings on the planet.
> 
> Another way of saying it is, AGI is not this upper bound on how smart a system could ever conceivably get, such that we should expect to see major breakthroughs before we even reach it; rather, it is more like a lower bound—a bare minimum that we must reach before we can even hope to see the kinds of breakthroughs you’re describing. So for that reason, it’s totally coherent to say that AGI is just 2-3 years away AND we haven’t seen those kinds of breakthroughs yet.

> I'm a software engineer and my job and workflow has changed entirely from what it was 4 years ago before ChatGPT came out. AI-native IDE's like Windsurf, Cursor, Claude Code, opencode, have fundamentally changed the nature of the job. I'm easily 2x-3x more productive now than I was before AI. I'm still reviewing all code changes, but for example when I submit a new chunk of code for a feature and then get feedback from my coworkers on things that should change, I have an automatic system setup that can pull in their feedback and implement the changes. That alone is a massive time saver. Other smaller features can be entirely automated as well. I have another system that can detect new tickets assigned to me and if they're relatively small straightforward features it can automatically spin up multiple agents in parallel to work on multiple tickets at once. Then again, I review the code, ensure it follows our standards and patterns, tweak it if necessary, then submit. Then get feedback from coworkers, which then goes into the automatic feedback resolution system. Now you're looking at iteration cycles that could previously have taken 3-5 days done in less than 3 hours.
